definition: A morphosyntactic alignment pattern in which the single argument of an intransitive verb (S) is treated like the object of a transitive verb (O), rather than like the subject (A) — the reverse of [[Nominative-Accusative Alignment]]. Found in languages such as Basque, Georgian, and many Australian languages.

A morphosyntactic alignment pattern in which S and A are treated alike (both nominative), and O is marked differently (accusative). The mirror pattern of [[Ergativity]], and the more common typological choice cross-linguistically.

A system in which a single language shows [[Ergativity]] in some grammatical contexts (e.g. past tense, or with certain persons) and [[Nominative-Accusative Alignment]] in others. Common conditioning factors include tense/aspect, person, and clause type.
